name: Representing size and socioeconomic status
what: An offeror is required to represent its size and socioeconomic status in writing to the [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer) at the time of initial offer (FAR 19.301-1) [427](#cite:427). The [representation](#term:representations-and-certifications) is made in the provision FAR 52.219-1, which includes the [small disadvantaged business](#term:sdb) box by reference to 13 CFR 124.1001 [373](#cite:373). Size is determined as of the written self-certification with the initial offer including price (13 CFR 121.404) [290](#cite:290). Bidding on a [set-aside](#term:set-aside), encouraging classification as small, or registering as small in a federal database is itself deemed a certification of size [295](#cite:295) [296](#cite:296).
applies_when: Every offer in which the firm claims small or program status [427](#cite:427). On a multiple-award contract, a firm small at contract award is small for each order, subject to the rerepresentation rules [427](#cite:427); a contract holder that cannot recertify for one order when the contracting officer asks may still be small for other orders where the contracting officer does not ask [290](#cite:290).
steps: Read the NAICS code on the [solicitation](#term:solicitation): the contracting officer assigns one code by principal purpose, and its size standard governs [425](#cite:425) [285](#cite:285)

Measure size against that standard: receipts averaged over five completed [fiscal years](#term:fiscal-year) [281](#cite:281); employees averaged over the preceding completed 24 calendar months [282](#cite:282); [affiliates](#term:affiliation) included [297](#cite:297)
The certification must be signed by an authorized official [295](#cite:295)

Know the penalties: a presumption of loss to the United States based on the total amount expended on the contract; suspension or [debarment](#term:responsibility); False Claims Act; criminal penalties under 15 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 645(d); with a limitation for unintentional errors, technical malfunctions and similar situations [295](#cite:295). FAR 52.219-1 states fine, imprisonment or both, suspension and debarment, and ineligibility for [Small Business Act](#term:small-business-act) programs [373](#cite:373)
A competitor, the contracting officer or [SBA](#term:sba) can challenge the representation by [size protest](#term:size-protest); private parties have five business days [294](#cite:294)

name: Recertification of size and program status (13 CFR 125.12)
what: 13 [CFR](#term:cfr) 125.12 is the unified rule on re-representing size and [8(a)](#term:eight-a), [HUBZone](#term:hubzone), [WOSB](#term:wosb)/EDWOSB and [SDVOSB](#term:sdvosb) status after certain events, and on what a disqualifying recertification costs the firm [291](#cite:291). It was added by the December 17, 2024 final rule and took effect January 17, 2026 [292](#cite:292). A firm that is small at award otherwise generally stays small for the life of the contract [290](#cite:290).
applies_when: Triggers: a merger, acquisition or sale that changes controlling interest (recertify within 30 calendar days); a contract longer than five years (no more than 120 days before the end of year five and before each later option); a contracting officer's request in a solicitation [291](#cite:291).
steps: Recertify size and program status within 30 calendar days of a merger, acquisition or sale [291](#cite:291)
A disqualifying recertification within 180 days after offer and before award makes the firm ineligible for that [set-aside](#term:set-aside) award [291](#cite:291)
On [multiple-award contracts](#term:idiq), a disqualifying recertification makes the firm ineligible for later set-aside or reserved orders; it stays eligible for unrestricted awards [291](#cite:291)
Exception: after a merger, acquisition or sale involving another small business, the firm stays eligible for set-aside or reserved orders [291](#cite:291)
Paragraph (g): events before January 17, 2026 keep eligibility for existing orders and options, but agencies cannot count them toward goals [291](#cite:291)
Recertify within 30 calendar days of the merger, acquisition or sale (13 CFR 125.12(a)) [291](#cite:291)

Before award: a triggering event within 180 days of offer and before award makes the firm ineligible for that single award; after 180 days the award may proceed (13 CFR 125.12(e)(2)(i)) [291](#cite:291)

Multiple-award contracts: after a merger with or acquisition by a firm that is not small, the contractor is ineligible for set-aside or reserved orders and options; after a merger between two small businesses it stays eligible but the orders do not count toward goals (13 CFR 125.12(e)(2)(ii)(B)) [291](#cite:291)
Long contracts: recertify no more than 120 days before the end of the fifth year and before each option thereafter (13 CFR 125.12(b)) [291](#cite:291)

Joint ventures: a joint venture may recertify as small where all parties are small at recertification, or the [protégé](#term:mentor-protege-sba) is small in a mentor-protégé joint venture (13 CFR 125.12(f)) [291](#cite:291); once the protégé is no longer small for the contract's [NAICS code](#term:naics) the joint venture cannot recertify as small [785](#cite:785)

steps: The twelve provisions of 13 CFR 125.8(b)(2): (1) purpose; (2) the small business as managing venturer with a named Responsible Manager; (3) the small business owns at least 51% of a separate-legal-entity joint venture; (4) profits commensurate with the work performed, or more; (5) a special bank account in the joint venture's name requiring the signature or consent of all parties; (6) itemised equipment, facilities and resources; (7) responsibilities for negotiation, labour and performance; (8) all parties obligated to complete performance despite a member's withdrawal; (9) accounting records kept by the managing venturer; (10) final records retained by the managing venturer; (11) annual performance statements to SBA not later than 45 days after each operating year; (12) a project-end statement no later than 90 days after completion [773](#cite:773)

Other partners may take part in commercially customary corporate-governance decisions; the Responsible Manager need not be an employee of the small business at offer if there is a signed letter of intent to be employed by it on award (13 CFR 125.8(b)(2)(ii)) [773](#cite:773)

Work share: the joint venture meets 13 CFR 125.6, and the protégé performs at least 40% of the work the joint venture performs, more than administrative or ministerial functions; work of the mentor and its [affiliates](#term:affiliation) at any subcontracting tier counts as the mentor's, and work by a [similarly situated](#term:similarly-situated-entity) [subcontractor](#term:prime-and-subcontractor) does not count toward the protégé's 40% (13 CFR 125.8(c)) [773](#cite:773)
Before performance: a written certification signed by an authorised official of each partner to the [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer) and SBA (13 CFR 125.8(d)) [773](#cite:773)

During and after: an annual performance-of-work report to the contracting officer and SBA and a completion report at the end of the contract (13 CFR 125.8(h)); SBA and its [Inspector General](#term:dod-ig) may inspect and copy the joint venture's records (13 CFR 125.8(g)) [773](#cite:773)

Program joint ventures: the certified firm is managing venturer, owns at least 51% and performs at least 40%, with quarterly financial statements not later than 45 days after each operating quarter and a project-end statement no later than 90 days after completion [774](#cite:774) [776](#cite:776) [778](#cite:778) [779](#cite:779); HUBZone and VOSB/SDVOSB joint ventures certify at offer as well as before performance or award [776](#cite:776) [779](#cite:779)

The joint venture itself: in writing, under its own name, identified as a joint venture in [SAM](#term:sam-gov) [770](#cite:770); with its own [UEI](#term:uei) and [CAGE code](#term:cage-code) [789](#cite:789)

Consequences: failing to have a compliant agreement, to perform to it or to the 40% rule, or to submit certifications or allow inspection are grounds for suspension or [debarment](#term:responsibility), and any person may report non-compliance to SBA or its OIG (13 CFR 125.8(i)-(j)) [773](#cite:773); a HUBZone or VOSB/SDVOSB joint venture can be protested for failing its section [777](#cite:777) [780](#cite:780)

The [eCFR](#term:ecfr) timeline shows the last amendment of 13 [CFR](#term:cfr) 121.103 on January 16, 2025 [770](#cite:770).
Final rule 88 FR 26164 (RIN 3245-AH70), effective May 30, 2023, added the ostensible subcontractor factors and the general-construction clarification [783](#cite:783).

name: Ostensible subcontractor rule and affiliation risk in teaming and joint ventures
what: An ostensible subcontractor is a [subcontractor](#term:prime-and-subcontractor) that is not a [similarly situated entity](#term:similarly-situated-entity) and performs primary and vital requirements of a contract or order, or is a subcontractor upon which the prime contractor is unusually reliant (13 CFR 121.103(h)(3)(i)) [706](#cite:706). Such a relationship makes the offeror ineligible as a small business; since final rule 89 FR 102448 (effective January 16, 2025) the offeror is ineligible rather than being treated as a joint venture [770](#cite:770) [292](#cite:292). Compliance is judged "as of the date of the final proposal revision for [negotiated acquisitions](#term:far-part-15) and final bid for sealed bidding" (13 CFR 121.404(f)) [771](#cite:771).
applies_when: A small prime on a set-aside relies on a subcontractor that is not similarly situated, such as a large or incumbent firm [706](#cite:706); and, for the wider affiliation rules, whenever firms team, joint venture or share owners, managers or revenue [770](#cite:770).
steps: Safe harbour for services, specialty trade construction and supplies: SBA will find no ostensible subcontractor where the prime, together with similarly situated small business subcontractors, meets the [limitations on subcontracting](#term:limitations-on-subcontracting) in 13 CFR 125.6 (13 CFR 121.103(h)(3)(iii)) [706](#cite:706) [770](#cite:770)

General construction: "the primary and vital requirements of the contract are the management, supervision and oversight of the project", not the construction work itself (13 CFR 121.103(h)(3)(iv)) [706](#cite:706) [770](#cite:770)
A prime may use a subcontractor's experience and [past performance](#term:cpars), including an incumbent's, and no single factor is determinative [706](#cite:706) [783](#cite:783)

Limitations on subcontracting: not more than 50% of the amount paid by the Government for services or supplies, 85% for general construction and 75% for special trade construction may go to firms that are not similarly situated; work a similarly situated subcontractor performs with its own employees is excluded from the cap and from the ostensible subcontractor rule; the penalty is the greater of $500,000 or the excess spent [424](#cite:424) [423](#cite:423)
[Contracting officers](#term:contracting-officer) may ask a small prime for information showing compliance with the limitations on subcontracting [711](#cite:711)

Joint ventures: a joint venture is ineligible where the managing partner will not perform 40% of the joint venture's work (13 CFR 121.103(h)(3)(v)) [706](#cite:706); after two years from its first award the partners of a joint venture are deemed [affiliated](#term:affiliation) for new offers, and each partner counts its proportionate share of the joint venture's receipts and employees [770](#cite:770)

Identity of interest (13 CFR 121.103(f)): family members who do business with each other are presumed affiliated, and economic dependence is presumed where a concern derived 70% or more of its receipts from another concern over the previous three [fiscal years](#term:fiscal-year); both presumptions are rebuttable [770](#cite:770)

Newly organized concern (13 CFR 121.103(g)): former officers or key employees who start a firm in the same or a related industry with assistance from the old firm; rebuttable by a clear line of fracture [770](#cite:770)

Exceptions: an SBA-approved [mentor-protégé](#term:mentor-protege-sba) agreement is not by itself a basis for affiliation (13 CFR 121.103(b)(6)); a [Small Business Teaming Arrangement](#term:teaming-agreement) on a bundled or [multiple-award contract](#term:idiq) above the substantial bundling threshold carries no affiliation if each member is small (13 CFR 121.103(b)(9)) [770](#cite:770)

Who can raise it: on a [set-aside](#term:set-aside), any offeror not eliminated for reasons unrelated to size, the contracting officer, or the SBA Government Contracting Area Director may file a [size protest](#term:size-protest) [772](#cite:772); [VOSB](#term:sdvosb)/SDVOSB undue-reliance [protests](#term:bid-protest) need credible evidence [780](#cite:780)

Pointer only, not regulation text: a law-firm explainer lists four reliance factors SBA's [Office of Hearings and Appeals](#term:oha) applies (the subcontractor is the ineligible incumbent; the prime plans to hire most of its workforce from it; the prime's managers previously worked for it on the incumbent contract; the prime lacks relevant experience) and says a finding causes affiliation for that contract only [760](#cite:760) [706](#cite:706)

name: Prompt payment and accelerated payment (what reaches a subcontractor)
what: The Prompt Payment clock is the Government's own deadline for paying its [prime contractor](#term:prime-and-subcontractor), with interest paid automatically when the Government is late [941](#cite:941). Treasury's pages speak of agencies paying vendors and do not address subcontractors [663](#cite:663). Two rules do reach a subcontractor. When the Government pays a prime on an accelerated basis, the prime must pass the payment on to its small-business subcontractors within 15 days, to the maximum extent practicable, without charging fees [661](#cite:661). On construction, every subcontract must carry a 7-day payment clause and an interest clause, flowed to lower tiers [942](#cite:942) [944](#cite:944).
applies_when: Accelerated payment: small-business subcontractors under a prime that receives accelerated payments; the substance of the clause flows to all subcontracts with small business concerns, including commercial products and services [661](#cite:661). Seven-day rule: subcontractors on federal construction contracts, with the same clauses in lower-tier subcontracts [942](#cite:942) [944](#cite:944).
steps: Invoice properly: the prime's 15-day duty runs after receipt of a proper invoice and all other required documentation from the small business subcontractor [661](#cite:661)

A subcontractor or supplier may tell the [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer) it has not been paid; the officer may determine whether the prime made payments in compliance with the subcontract, and may encourage timely payment or reduce or suspend progress payments ([FAR](#term:far) 32.112-1) [951](#cite:951)
If the prime's certification of payment was inaccurate, "the contracting officer shall initiate administrative or other remedial action" [951](#cite:951)
how_it_works: Government to prime: invoice payment is due on the later of the 30th day after the billing office receives a proper invoice or the 30th day after Government acceptance (FAR 32.904(b)(1)) [941](#cite:941)
Government to prime, construction: progress payments are due 14 days after receipt of a proper payment request (FAR 32.904(d)(1)(i)) [941](#cite:941)
"The designated payment office will pay an interest penalty automatically, without request from the contractor" (FAR 32.907) [941](#cite:941)

Interest rate: "For the period beginning July 1, 2026, and ending on December 31, 2026, the prompt payment interest rate is 4-3/4 per centum per annum." (91 [FR](#term:federal-register) 42594) [945](#cite:945); Treasury's page gives the same figure as 4.75% [663](#cite:663)

[Accelerated payment](#term:accelerated-payment) policy: agencies "provide accelerated payments, to the fullest extent permitted by law, with a goal of 15 days after receipt of a proper invoice"; it covers small business contractors and prime contractors that subcontract with small business, if the prime agrees to pass payment on within 15 days [662](#cite:662)

For civilian agencies the goal applies only when a specific payment date is not established by contract; DoD has a parallel paragraph under separate statutory authority [662](#cite:662) [937](#cite:937)

The prime pays small business subcontractors "within 15 days after receipt of accelerated payments from the Government", "to the maximum extent practicable", after receipt of a proper invoice and all other required documentation from the small business subcontractor [661](#cite:661)
No further consideration or fees may be charged to the subcontractor [661](#cite:661)
"The acceleration of payments under this clause does not provide any new rights under the Prompt Payment Act." [661](#cite:661)
FAR 52.232-40 is on both commercial [flow-down](#term:flow-down) lists [695](#cite:695) [955](#cite:955)

Construction: the prime pays subcontractors for satisfactory performance "not later than 7 days from receipt of payment out of such amounts as are paid to the Contractor"; interest accrues from the day after the required payment date, at the rate under 41 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 7109 [942](#cite:942)

Construction: the parties may agree retainage; withholding for documented deficiencies is permitted with prior written notice; after a deficiency is corrected, payment is due within 7 days or interest accrues [942](#cite:942)

Construction: each progress-payment request carries the prime's certification that "All payments due to subcontractors and suppliers from previous payments received under the contract have been made" [943](#cite:943)

Interest a prime owes a subcontractor is not an obligation of the Government and cannot be claimed as a cost [942](#cite:942); a payment dispute between a contractor and a subcontractor is not a dispute to which the United States is a party [944](#cite:944)

[Cost-reimbursement contracts](#term:cost-reimbursement-contract): a prime may bill the Government for subcontract costs it has not yet paid only if it pays "ordinarily within 30 days of the submission of the Contractor's payment request to the Government" [946](#cite:946)

History: a DoD rule effective April 8, 2020 created [DFARS](#term:dfars) 252.232-7017 (section 852, [NDAA](#term:ndaa) FY2019) [939](#cite:939); CAAC Letter 2020-02 authorised a civilian [class deviation](#term:class-deviation) in April 2020 (section 873, NDAA FY2020) [938](#cite:938); the FAR [final rule](#term:final-rule) (88 FR 9730, FAR Case 2020-007) took effect March 16, 2023 [937](#cite:937); the DFARS page now reads "252.232-7017 Reserved." name: Miller Act payment bond claim
what: On federal construction above the threshold the prime furnishes a [payment bond](#term:miller-act), which protects those supplying labor and material [947](#cite:947). An unpaid [subcontractor](#term:prime-and-subcontractor) or supplier claims on the bond by suit in federal district court, after a 90-day wait and within one year [948](#cite:948).
applies_when: A person who furnished labor or material on a bonded federal construction contract and has not been paid in full within 90 days after the last labor or material; a person with a direct contract with a subcontractor but none with the prime must also give the prime written notice [948](#cite:948).
steps: Ask the [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer) for the surety's name and address, the penal amount, and a copy of the payment bond; a reasonable copying fee is allowed [950](#cite:950)
A certified copy of the bond and contract goes to anyone who files an affidavit of non-payment for labor or material [950](#cite:950) [948](#cite:948)
If second tier, give the prime written notice within 90 days from the last labor or material [948](#cite:948)
File suit in U.S. District Court after the 90 days and no later than one year after the last labor or material [948](#cite:948)
how_it_works: Threshold in the [FAR](#term:far): it "requires performance and payment bonds for any construction contract exceeding $150,000" [644](#cite:644)
Threshold in the statute as read: "Before any contract of more than $100,000 is awarded for the construction, alteration, or repair of any public building or public work" [947](#cite:947)

Contracts over $35,000 and up to $150,000: the contracting officer selects two or more payment protections (payment bond, irrevocable letter of credit, tripartite escrow agreement, certificates of deposit, other security) [644](#cite:644)

Amount: above $150,000 the payment bond is 100 percent of the original contract price plus 100 percent of any increase, and "the amount of the payment bond must be no less than the amount of the performance bond" [949](#cite:949); the statute sets it at the total amount payable under the contract unless the contracting officer finds that impractical in writing [947](#cite:947)
The inflation adjustment effective October 1, 2025 excluded the performance and payment bond thresholds [340](#cite:340)
A civil action may be brought if the claimant is not paid in full within 90 days after the last labor or material (40 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 3133(b)(1)) [948](#cite:948)
Second tier: written notice to the prime within 90 days from the last labor or material, by any means that provides written, third-party verification (40 U.S.C. 3133(b)(2)) [948](#cite:948)

Suit is in the name of the United States for the use of the claimant, in the U.S. District Court for the district where the contract was to be performed, and "must be brought no later than one year after the day on which the last of the labor was performed or material was supplied" [948](#cite:948)
A waiver of the right to sue is void unless in writing, signed by the person waiving, and executed after the labor or material was furnished [948](#cite:948)

Pay-when-paid: the Ninth Circuit held that a "pay when and if paid" [clause](#term:clause-numbering) did not bar the Miller Act payment bond claim and that a waiver of Miller Act rights must be clear and explicit; one circuit only [952](#cite:952)

Related: [SBA](#term:sba) guarantees bid, payment, performance and ancillary bonds for small contractors, on non-federal contracts up to $9 million and federal contracts up to $14 million, with a guarantee fee of 0.6% of the contract price for performance and payment bonds; the page does not say whether subcontracts qualify [645](#cite:645)

name: Flow-down clauses
what: A [flow-down](#term:flow-down) is a clause in the prime contract that the prime must repeat in its [subcontracts](#term:prime-and-subcontractor). For a commercial subcontract the [FAR](#term:far) lists the clauses a prime must flow down and says "the Contractor may flow down to subcontracts for [commercial products](#term:commercial-product) or commercial services a minimal number of additional clauses necessary to satisfy its contractual obligations" [695](#cite:695). Where the prime contract itself is commercial, "the Contractor is not required to flow down any FAR clause, other than those in this paragraph (e)(1)" [955](#cite:955).
applies_when: Any subcontract under a federal prime contract; the required lists apply to subcontracts for commercial products and commercial services [695](#cite:695) [955](#cite:955), and each other clause sets its own trigger.
how_it_works: DoD: no FAR or DFARS clause flows to a commercial subcontract unless that clause requires it ([DFARS](#term:dfars) 252.244-7000, as paraphrased by the fetch) [956](#cite:956)

Basic safeguarding (FAR 52.204-21): fifteen safeguarding requirements, flowed to subcontracts, including commercial ones other than [COTS](#term:cots), "in which the subcontractor may have [Federal contract information](#term:fci-cui) residing in or transiting through its information system" [617](#cite:617)

[DFARS 252.204-7012](#term:nist-sp-800-171): included in subcontracts for operationally critical support or involving covered defense information, including commercial subcontracts, "without alteration, except to identify the parties"; the sub notifies the prime when it asks the [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer) to vary from a NIST SP 800-171 requirement and gives the prime the DoD-assigned incident report number; cyber incidents are reported within 72 hours of discovery [618](#cite:618)

[CMMC](#term:cmmc) (DFARS 252.204-7021, NOV 2025): flows to subcontracts involving Federal contract information or controlled unclassified information, excluding COTS items; before awarding, the prime checks that the sub holds a "current CMMC status at the [CMMC level](#term:cmmc-levels) that is appropriate for the information that is being flowed down"; affirmation of continuous compliance before subcontract award and annually [621](#cite:621)

Trafficking (FAR 52.222-50): "The Contractor shall include the substance of this clause, including this paragraph (i), in all subcontracts and in all contracts with agents."; the compliance plan applies to any portion of a contract or subcontract over $700,000 for non-COTS supplies acquired, or services performed, outside the United States (figure as displayed; recheck) [654](#cite:654)

[E-Verify](#term:e-verify) (FAR 52.222-54): subcontracts for services (other than commercial services that are part of a COTS purchase) or construction, valued at "more than $3,500", with work performed in the United States [647](#cite:647)

[Service Contract Labor Standards](#term:service-contract-act) (FAR 52.222-41): "The Contractor agrees to insert this clause in all subcontracts subject to the Service Contract Labor Standards statute."; withholding, payment suspension and termination are available for underpayment of wages or fringe benefits [958](#cite:958)

Construction labor (FAR 52.222-11): eleven named labor clauses go into each construction subcontract; "The prime Contractor shall be responsible for compliance by any subcontractor or lower tier subcontractor"; an SF 1413 within 14 days after contract award for each subcontract [959](#cite:959)

[Accelerated payment](#term:accelerated-payment) (FAR 52.232-40): the substance flows to all subcontracts with [small business concerns](#term:size-standard), including commercial products and services [661](#cite:661)
Technical data and software (DFARS 252.227-7013 and 252.227-7014): flow without alteration, except to identify the parties [968](#cite:968) [970](#cite:970)

[Certified cost or pricing data](#term:certified-cost-or-pricing-data): the prime inserts FAR 52.215-12 or 52.215-13 in each subcontract that "exceeds the threshold for submission of certified cost or pricing data in FAR 15.403-4(a)(1)" [960](#cite:960) [961](#cite:961); the threshold is "$2.5 million for prime contracts awarded on or after July 1, 2018" ($950,000 before that date) and reaches a subcontract at any tier if the contractor and each higher-tier subcontractor were required to furnish certified data [962](#cite:962)

Subcontractor data goes to the Government when the subcontract is $20 million or more, or both above the threshold and more than 10 percent of the prime's proposed price: "the contractor shall submit, or cause to be submitted by the subcontractor(s), certified cost or pricing data to the Government" [963](#cite:963)

Consent to subcontract (FAR 52.244-2): consent is not a determination of the acceptability of subcontract terms or of cost allowability; "No subcontract or modification thereof placed under this contract shall provide for payment on a cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost basis"; the prime gives immediate written notice of any suit and prompt notice of any claim by a subcontractor [957](#cite:957)

Thresholds changed on October 1, 2025 (90 [FR](#term:federal-register) 41872, FAR Case 2024-001): [simplified acquisition threshold](#term:simplified-acquisition-threshold) $250,000 to $350,000; certified cost or pricing data $2,000,000 to $2,500,000; [subcontracting plan](#term:subcontracting-plan) $750,000 to $900,000 [340](#cite:340)

A prime's own terms, one company's example: Lockheed Martin's published general provisions for commercial subcontracts set payment terms net 45 days, New York governing law with FAR-derived provisions "construed and interpreted according to the federal common law of government contracts", stop-work for up to 90 days on written notice, and termination for convenience at any time; an illustration from one company, not representative of all primes [965](#cite:965)

name: Data rights as a subcontractor
what: The rules on what the Government and the prime can do with technical data, software and inventions a [subcontractor](#term:prime-and-subcontractor) brings or creates. For DoD work, "10 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 3771 provides subcontractors at all tiers the same protection for their rights in data as is provided to prime contractors." [969](#cite:969). Under the civilian clause, "The Contractor shall obtain from its subcontractors all data and rights therein necessary to fulfill the Contractor's obligations to the Government under this contract." [966](#cite:966)
applies_when: A subcontract under which technical data or software is delivered to the Government, where the DoD clauses flow without alteration [968](#cite:968) [970](#cite:970), and any subcontract for experimental, developmental or research work, where the patent rights clause flows [967](#cite:967).
steps: Give the prime, before the offer goes in, the entries for its assertions list: data or software to be furnished with restrictions; basis for assertion; asserted rights category; name of person asserting restrictions [971](#cite:971)
Use the legend the clause prescribes; the DoD legends name the contract number, contractor name and address [968](#cite:968) [970](#cite:970)
how_it_works: DoD policy (DFARS 227.7103-15): subcontractors may deal directly with the Government on validation of their markings (10 U.S.C. 3782) and cannot be made to give up rights as a condition of award; clauses to flow: 252.227-7013, 252.227-7025, 252.227-7028, 252.227-7037 [969](#cite:969)

DFARS 252.227-7013 (AUG 2025), paragraph (l): flows without alteration, except to identify the parties; a subcontractor's technical data may be submitted directly to the Government rather than through a higher tier; primes "shall not use their power to award contracts as economic leverage to obtain rights in technical data from their subcontractors or suppliers" [968](#cite:968)
Software (DFARS 252.227-7014): the prime must "require its subcontractors or suppliers to do so, without alteration, except to identify the parties" [970](#cite:970)
Private expense: developed exclusively at private expense means costs charged to indirect cost pools, costs not allocated to a Government contract, or any combination [968](#cite:968)

Assertions list (DFARS 252.227-7017): covers assertions by the offeror, its subcontractors or suppliers, and potential subcontractors or suppliers; it is submitted as an attachment to the offer and carries the warning "may render the offer ineligible for award" [971](#cite:971)

Civilian clause (FAR 52.227-14): if a subcontractor refuses terms giving the Government the required rights, the prime notifies the [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer) and does not award without written authorization [966](#cite:966)

Civilian clause: the contractor may withhold qualifying limited rights data and restricted computer software, identifying what is withheld and furnishing form, fit and function data instead; the clause as returned contains no express right for a subcontractor to deliver directly to the Government [966](#cite:966)

Markings: unauthorized markings can be cancelled or ignored after a 60-day written inquiry procedure [966](#cite:966); the DoD limited rights and restricted rights legends name the contract number, contractor name and address [968](#cite:968) [970](#cite:970)

Patents (FAR 52.227-11): the substance is included in all subcontracts for experimental, developmental or research work; "The Contractor shall not, as part of the consideration for awarding the subcontract, obtain rights in the subcontractor's subject inventions."; disclosure within 2 months, election to retain title within 2 years, patent application within 1 year after election [967](#cite:967)

Proposal data (FAR 52.215-1(e)): a title-page legend plus a per-sheet legend: "Use or disclosure of data contained on this sheet is subject to the restriction on the title page of this proposal." [972](#cite:972)

[SBIR](#term:sbir)/[STTR](#term:sttr): [data rights](#term:sbir-data-rights) apply to all SBIR/STTR awards, including subcontracts or subgrants (Policy Directive § 8(b)(2)); "A subcontract to a Federally-funded prime contract may be a [Phase III award](#term:phase-iii)." [5](#cite:5)

SBIR/STTR under DoD (DFARS 252.227-7018, AUG 2025): protection begins on the date of award of the contract under which the data are generated and ends 20 years after that date; "After the SBIR/STTR data protection period expiration date shown above, the Government has perpetual government purpose rights"; paragraph (l) carries the unaltered [flow-down](#term:flow-down), the leverage ban and direct delivery by subcontractors [24](#cite:24)

pending_changes.text: [FAR](#term:far) Part 33 ([protests](#term:bid-protest), disputes and appeals) is in the first batch of FAR-overhaul [proposed rules](#term:proposed-rule) issued June 23, 2026; comments were due July 23, 2026 [408](#cite:408).

Part 44 is in use by agency [class deviation](#term:class-deviation). The Department of Labor's (memo dated November 19, 2025; effective November 3, 2025) retains 52.244-2 with no text changes and cuts the consent review checklist from 13 points to four situations; the deviation numbering of FAR 44.203 was not read [983](#cite:983).

conflicts: Secondary only: a law-firm note reports ASBCA decisions in Sauer Inc., No. 62295 (August 13, 2025 and November 18, 2025) accepting conditional liability, where the prime agrees to pay the sub as and when it recovers from the Government, as satisfying the Severin doctrine; the Board decisions were not fetched [980](#cite:980).

Secondary only and not current law: a 2019 commentary describes a bill-stage provision (section 831 of a 2020 NDAA draft) for a formal OSDBU non-payment process; enactment was not verified [982](#cite:982).
15 U.S.C. 644(k) was read on Cornell LII and truncated at duty (16); later duties were not read [374](#cite:374).
name: Disputes with a prime
what: A [subcontractor](#term:prime-and-subcontractor) has no contract with the Government. [Contract Disputes Act](#term:contract-disputes-act) claims are claims by a contractor, defined as "a party to a Federal Government contract other than the Federal Government" [976](#cite:976) [977](#cite:977). The Federal Circuit put it this way: "Government consents to be sued only by those with whom it has privity of contract, which it does not have with subcontractors." [979](#cite:979)
applies_when: Any subcontractor in dispute with its prime, or with a claim that must travel through the prime because the Government has no privity with subcontractors [979](#cite:979) [978](#cite:978).
steps: A subcontractor may assert non-payment to the [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer), who may look into it and may encourage payment or reduce or suspend the prime's progress payments [951](#cite:951)

The prime "will not prohibit a subcontractor from discussing with the Contracting Officer any material matter pertaining to payment to or utilization of a subcontractor" [437](#cite:437); [SBA](#term:sba)'s rule says the same [704](#cite:704)
how_it_works: "Each claim by a contractor against the Federal Government relating to a contract shall be submitted to the contracting officer for a decision."; in writing, within 6 years after accrual [977](#cite:977)
Pass-through: a prime may sue for its subcontractor's costs; under the Severin doctrine the burden is on the Government to prove the prime is not responsible to the subcontractor [979](#cite:979)

FAR 44.203: the contracting officer will not consent to subcontracts obligating him to deal directly with the subcontractor; a subcontract may give an indirect appeal, meaning "assertion by the subcontractor of the prime contractor's right to appeal or the prosecution of an appeal by the prime contractor on the subcontractor's behalf", and may provide that prime and subcontractor are equally bound by the contracting officer's or board's decision [978](#cite:978)
The prime gives the contracting officer immediate written notice of any suit and prompt notice of any claim by a subcontractor [957](#cite:957)

[GAO](#term:gao): an interested party is an actual or prospective bidder or offeror (4 [CFR](#term:cfr) 21.0(a)(1)); "GAO will not consider a protest of the award or proposed award of a subcontract" except on agency request (21.5(h)); contract administration is outside GAO's protest function (21.5(a)) [467](#cite:467)

Construction payment: interest owed by a prime is not a federal obligation, and contractor–subcontractor disputes are not disputes with the United States (31 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 3905(i)-(j)) [944](#cite:944)

[OSDBU](#term:osdbu): each agency's small business office has a statutory duty covering payments, late payment interest penalties, and "information regarding payments due to such concerns from an executive agency or a contractor" (15 U.S.C. 644(k)(6)) [374](#cite:374)
SBA National Ombudsman: takes small-business comments about federal agency enforcement (fines, audits, inspections); nothing on its page offers help with a prime contractor [981](#cite:981)

[Subcontracting plan](#term:subcontracting-plan): failure to comply in good faith is a material breach (FAR 52.219-9(k)) [437](#cite:437); liquidated damages are "the actual dollar amount by which the Contractor failed to achieve each subcontract goal" [694](#cite:694)

Plan assurances that protect small subcontractors: a good-faith effort to buy from the small businesses used in preparing the bid or proposal, with a written explanation within 30 days of contract completion if not; unsuccessful small business subcontract offerors are told the name and location of the apparent successful offeror [437](#cite:437)
A prime that names a small business as a subcontractor in a proposal must notify it in writing beforehand (13 CFR 125.3(c)(8)) [704](#cite:704)

SBA [Commercial Market Representatives](#term:cmr) conduct Subcontracting Program Compliance Reviews of large primes, per SBA's June 2010 handbook; a non-compliant prime "may be found in material breach of contract and terminated for default, or liquidated damages may be imposed" [900](#cite:900)

pending_changes.text: FAR-overhaul numbering for [FAR](#term:far) 15.305 and 42.1502 was not read in this slice; the codified pages cited show [FAC](#term:fac) 2026-01, effective 2026-03-13 [984](#cite:984) [603](#cite:603).

name: Past performance as a subcontractor
what: [CPARS](#term:cpars) does not rate [subcontractors](#term:prime-and-subcontractor): "Evaluations are not completed for subcontractors." [985](#cite:985). A small first-tier subcontractor on a prime contract that had a [subcontracting plan](#term:subcontracting-plan) may ask its prime for a written performance rating to use in its own bids [781](#cite:781).
applies_when: Small first-tier subcontractors where the prime contract had a subcontracting plan, and small joint-venture members [781](#cite:781).
steps: Request the written rating from the prime within 30 days after the period of performance is complete [781](#cite:781)
The prime has 15 calendar days to respond; the subcontractor may notify the [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer) if the prime does not comply [781](#cite:781)
how_it_works: CPARS: the prime is assessed on how it manages subcontractors (Guidance § 2.13); a formal [joint venture](#term:joint-venture) gets a single evaluation under its own [Unique Entity ID](#term:uei), otherwise only the named prime is evaluated (§ 2.5) [985](#cite:985)
The request goes to the prime within 30 days after completion of the period of performance; the prime responds within 15 calendar days of the request [781](#cite:781)
Scale: Exceptional, Very Good, Satisfactory, Marginal, Unsatisfactory; factors: technical (quality), cost control, schedule/timeliness, management or business relations, other [781](#cite:781)
The agency "shall consider the concern's experience and rating of past performance as a first-tier subcontractor" [781](#cite:781)
A small joint-venture member may request and use such a rating in the same way [781](#cite:781)

Origin: [SBA](#term:sba) [final rule](#term:final-rule) 87 [FR](#term:federal-register) 43731, effective August 22, 2022, implementing section 868 of [NDAA](#term:ndaa) FY2021; the final rule dropped a three-year age limit on the performance used [713](#cite:713)

A small prime's team: when a small prime's offer identifies a team of small business first-tier subcontractors, "the head of the agency must consider the capabilities, past performance, and experience of each first tier subcontractor that is part of the team" if the prime's own do not independently suffice (13 [CFR](#term:cfr) 125.2(g)) [431](#cite:431)

FAR 15.305(a)(2)(iii): evaluators should take into account predecessor companies, key personnel, and subcontractors performing major or critical aspects; with no record, "the offeror may not be evaluated favorably or unfavorably on past performance" [984](#cite:984)

Joint ventures: the agency "must consider work done and qualifications held individually by each partner to the joint venture" (13 CFR 125.8(e)) [773](#cite:773); a small member "cannot identify and use as its own experience and past performance work that was performed exclusively by other partners to the joint venture" [713](#cite:713)

FAR 42.1502 states evaluation thresholds for contracts and orders held by the contractor (each contract or order exceeding the [simplified acquisition threshold](#term:simplified-acquisition-threshold); construction contracts of $900,000 or more; architect-engineer services contracts of $45,000 or more); nothing returned provides for evaluating a subcontractor [603](#cite:603)

pending_changes.text: [SBA](#term:sba) [proposed rule](#term:proposed-rule) 89 [FR](#term:federal-register) 103709 (RIN 3245-AI09) would bring 13 [CFR](#term:cfr) 125.3 into line with section 862 of the FY2024 [NDAA](#term:ndaa) ([Pub. L.](#term:public-law) 118-31) by cutting the reporting trigger from 90 to 30 days and adding a duty to cooperate: "The [prime contractor](#term:prime-and-subcontractor) has the duty to cooperate with the [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer) until the subcontractor receives full payment". Comments were due February 18, 2025; no [final rule](#term:final-rule) was found in this sweep [714](#cite:714).

FAR-overhaul numbering for Parts 19 and 42 and for [clauses](#term:clause-numbering) 52.219-8, 52.219-9 and 52.242-5 was not read in this slice; the codified pages cited show [FAC](#term:fac) 2026-01, effective 2026-03-13 [698](#cite:698). Per SBA Advocacy, the first batch of FAR-overhaul proposed rules (June 23, 2026) does not include [Part 19](#term:far-part-19) [408](#cite:408).

conflicts: Late-payment trigger: more than 30 days past due in 15 U.S.C. 637(d)(13), 2024 edition [953](#cite:953); more than 90 days in FAR 52.242-5 as displayed [698](#cite:698) and in 13 CFR 125.3(c)(5) as displayed [704](#cite:704). Whether SBA finalised RIN 3245-AI09, and whether a FAR case is open, was not established [714](#cite:714).

Subcontracting-plan threshold: $900,000 and $2 million for construction in FAR 19.702 [435](#cite:435) and in the 2025 inflation rule [340](#cite:340); $750,000 and $1,500,000 in 13 CFR 125.3 as it reads [704](#cite:704).
name: Late-payment reporting by the prime
what: On a contract that requires a [subcontracting plan](#term:subcontracting-plan), a prime that pays a small-business subcontractor a reduced price or pays late must notify the contracting officer in writing and give the reason [953](#cite:953) [698](#cite:698). An unjustified failure counts in the prime's [past performance](#term:cpars) evaluation [953](#cite:953) [604](#cite:604).
applies_when: Small-business subcontractors under a prime whose contract requires a subcontracting plan [953](#cite:953). Plans are required above $900,000 generally and $2 million for construction under FAR 19.702, and are not required from small business concerns [435](#cite:435).
steps: The duty to report is the prime's; a subcontractor that is unpaid may itself assert non-payment to the contracting officer, who may encourage payment or reduce or suspend the prime's progress payments [951](#cite:951)
how_it_works: Statute (2024 edition): written notice when the prime pays a reduced price or "the payment to a subcontractor is more than 30 days past due for goods or services provided for the covered contract", for work the agency has paid the prime for [953](#cite:953)

FAR clause as displayed: untimely payment is "a payment that is more than 90 days past due under the terms and conditions of a subcontract", for supplies and services for which the Government has paid the prime [698](#cite:698)
SBA regulation as displayed (13 CFR 125.3(c)(5)): the prime notifies the contracting officer if it pays a reduced price or payment is more than 90 days past due [704](#cite:704)
Written notice to the contracting officer not later than 14 days after the event, giving the reason [698](#cite:698)
The subcontracting plan carries an assurance to pay small business subcontractors on time and notify the contracting officer of reduced or untimely payment (FAR 52.219-9(d)(15)) [437](#cite:437)
Primes must "establish procedures to ensure the timely payment of amounts due pursuant to the terms of their subcontracts" ([FAR](#term:far) 52.219-8) [693](#cite:693)
Past performance: small business subcontracting, including reduced or untimely payments to small business subcontractors, is an evaluation factor [604](#cite:604)

FAPIIS: a report is made when a contractor has "a history of three or more unjustified reduced or untimely payments to small business subcontractors under a single contract within a 12-month period", within 3 calendar days (FAR 42.1503(h)) [604](#cite:604)

Statute: the contracting officer shall consider the unjustified failure in evaluating the prime and may enter or modify past performance information before or after close-out; the prime must cooperate once an unjustified failure is determined [953](#cite:953)
"The contractor may not prohibit a subcontractor from discussing any material matter pertaining to payment or utilization with the contracting officer" (13 CFR 125.3(c)(1)(iii)) [704](#cite:704)

Origin: FAR final rule 81 FR 93481 (FAR Case 2014-004), effective January 19, 2017, implementing section 1334 of the Small Business Jobs Act of 2010; it created FAR 52.242-5 and the FAPIIS reporting [954](#cite:954)

pending_changes.text: 13 [CFR](#term:cfr) 125.12 shows a last amendment date of 2026-09-29; the content of that amendment was not identified, and paragraph (g) uses January 17, 2026 as a transition date [291](#cite:291).
FAR-overhaul numbering for [FAR](#term:far) 52.219-8 was not read in this slice; the codified page cited shows [FAC](#term:fac) 2026-01, effective 2026-03-13 [693](#cite:693).

name: Size at subcontract
what: "For subcontracting purposes, a concern must qualify as small as of the date that it certifies that it is small for the [subcontract](#term:prime-and-subcontractor)." [986](#cite:986). The subcontractor is small if "it does not exceed the [size standard](#term:size-standard) for the [NAICS code](#term:naics) that the prime contractor believes best describes the product or service being acquired" by the subcontract [989](#cite:989).
applies_when: Each time a firm represents itself as small for a subcontract: "A subcontractor must still qualify and self-certify as a small business at the time it submits its offer" [990](#cite:990).
steps: Check size as of the date of certifying for each subcontract, against the NAICS code the prime assigns to it [986](#cite:986) [989](#cite:989)
how_it_works: Primes may rely on [SAM](#term:sam-gov) as an accurate [representation](#term:representations-and-certifications) of size and ownership [990](#cite:990); under FAR 52.219-8 a prime may accept a size representation in writing or through SAM, and contractors may not require the use of SAM for size or status representations [693](#cite:693)

Receipts: all revenue from whatever source, averaged over the most recently completed five [fiscal years](#term:fiscal-year), with [affiliates](#term:affiliation)' average receipts added; "All other items, such as subcontractor costs ... may not be excluded from receipts." [987](#cite:987)

Employees: the average "based upon numbers of employees for each of the pay periods for the preceding completed 24 calendar months", including employees of domestic and foreign affiliates [988](#cite:988)

[Protest](#term:bid-protest) and penalties: a subcontractor's size may be protested by the [contracting officer](#term:contracting-officer), the prime, the [SBA](#term:sba) official or any other interested party; misrepresentation carries suspension or [debarment](#term:responsibility), False Claims Act civil penalties, criminal penalties [990](#cite:990)

Competitive subcontracts over the [simplified acquisition threshold](#term:simplified-acquisition-threshold): unsuccessful offerors are told the name and location of the apparent successful offeror [990](#cite:990)

[Recertification](#term:recertification) on prime contracts (13 CFR 125.12): "Recertification of size and small business program status is required within 30 calendar days of a merger, acquisition, or sale of or by a concern"; on long-term contracts, no more than 120 days before the end of the fifth year and before each option thereafter; growth alone between those events is not listed as a trigger in what was returned [291](#cite:291)

Dependence on one customer: a concern that derived 70% or more of its receipts from another concern over the previous three fiscal years is presumed affiliated with it, rebuttably (13 CFR 121.103(f)(2)) [770](#cite:770)

[Joint ventures](#term:joint-venture): "a specific joint venture generally may not be awarded contracts beyond a two-year period, starting from the date of the award of the first contract" without the partners being deemed affiliated [770](#cite:770)

[Ostensible subcontractor](#term:ostensible-subcontractor): one that is not a [similarly situated entity](#term:similarly-situated-entity) and performs primary and vital requirements, or on which the prime is unusually reliant (13 CFR 121.103(h)(3)) [770](#cite:770)

pending_changes.text: Not specific to [OTs](#term:other-transaction): [Pub. L. 119-60](#term:ndaa) carries a section headed "Sec. 875 Ability to withhold contract payments during period of pendancy of a [bid protest](#term:bid-protest)" (heading read; body not read) [806](#cite:806). Law-firm summaries say DoD may withhold up to 5% of payments to an incumbent during a GAO protest and that a [DFARS](#term:dfars) revision is required [806](#cite:806) [1107](#cite:1107).

name: Protesting an other transaction at GAO (limited jurisdiction)
what: [GAO](#term:gao) "generally does not review" protests of awards, or [solicitations](#term:solicitation) for awards, of agreements other than [procurement contracts](#term:grant) [1038](#cite:1038). One door stays open: "GAO does, however, review protests alleging that an agency is improperly using a non-procurement instrument to procure goods or services." [1038](#cite:1038). When it does look, GAO reviews only whether the agency's use of its discretionary authority was proper, "i.e., knowing and authorized" [1074](#cite:1074).
applies_when: A firm wants to challenge an OT solicitation or award on the ground that the agency has no authority to use an OT for it, or is using one where a procurement contract is required [1038](#cite:1038) [1075](#cite:1075).
steps: Timeliness rule applied in Oracle: filing within 10 days of learning of the award (4 [CFR](#term:cfr) 21.2(a)(2)) [1074](#cite:1074)
Where an agency has an agency-level protest process for OTs, the solicitation states it [1049](#cite:1049)
how_it_works: What GAO will hear: "a protester argues that an agency is improperly using its other transaction authority to procure goods or services, we will review the matter" (ACI Technologies, B-417011, January 17, 2019; denied in part and dismissed in part) [1075](#cite:1075)

What GAO will not hear: how the agency evaluated proposals. MD Helicopters, B-417379 (April 4, 2019) "is dismissed because our Office generally does not review protests of awards, or solicitations for awards, of other transaction agreements" [1076](#cite:1076)
GAO's reason: agreements under OT authority "are not procurement contracts and do not fall under the provisions of the [Federal Acquisition Regulation](#term:far)" [1076](#cite:1076)

Sustained once: Oracle America, B-416061 (May 31, 2018). "the Army did not properly exercise the authority granted to it under the statute" when it awarded a [follow-on production](#term:follow-on-production) OTA: the prototype OTA had no follow-on provision, and the [prototype project](#term:prototype-ot) was not complete at award [1074](#cite:1074)
Timeliness in Oracle: the protest was timely because filed within 10 days of learning of the award (4 CFR 21.2(a)(2)) [1074](#cite:1074)

Other GAO dismissals for lack of jurisdiction or untimeliness: Blade Strategies B-416752 (Sept. 24, 2018); System Architecture Info. Tech. B-418721 (June 2, 2020); Spartan Medical B-419503 (Feb. 26, 2021) [1080](#cite:1080)

An [ARPA-H](#term:arpa-h) page indexes thirteen GAO decisions on OTs, with copies, from Exploration Partners B-298804 (Dec 2006) to PredictiveIQ B-421436.2 (Jul 2023), Lunar Resources B-421936 (Nov 2023) and [HHS](#term:agency-abbreviations) fiscal law B-333150 (Apr 2024) [1069](#cite:1069)

Agency-level protest: "There is nothing prohibiting agencies from establishing a process for an agency-level protest."; agencies that set one up state it in the solicitation, and the [Agreements Officer](#term:contracting-officer) confers with counsel at once when a protest arrives [1049](#cite:1049)
ARPA-H's plain statement: "OTs can be protested, but what can be protested and where protests must be filed is more complicated and less established"; GAO has limited jurisdiction [1067](#cite:1067)
DARPA's and ARPA-H's training both list the procurement protest process among the things that do not apply to OTs [1063](#cite:1063) [1066](#cite:1066)

conflicts: The line of cases is not uniform: SpaceX (2019) found no jurisdiction [1080](#cite:1080); Raytheon (2025) calls the court the de facto forum [1081](#cite:1081); Telesto (2025) limits review to compliance with the OT statutes and the solicitation's terms [1082](#cite:1082).

Citations: the reporter citation for Independent Rough Terrain Center (172 Fed. Cl. 250 (2024)) and the Westlaw citation for Raytheon (2025 WL 583350) come from a law-firm alert [1084](#cite:1084); Raytheon was read on Justia, not the court's site [1081](#cite:1081); Hydraulics, Kinemetrics and SpaceX were not read directly [1080](#cite:1080).
name: Protesting an other transaction at the Court of Federal Claims (and the district courts)
what: The [Court of Federal Claims](#term:bid-protest) has taken jurisdiction over several [OT](#term:other-transaction) protests, and one judge has called it "the de facto forum for bid protests involving 'other transactions' (OTs) and 'other transaction agreements' (OTAs) awarded under 10 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) §§ 4021–22" [1081](#cite:1081) [1069](#cite:1069). A later decision drew a narrower line: the court can review whether an OT complies with the OT statutes and the [solicitation](#term:solicitation)'s own terms, but "There is no authority to review an agency's conduct of the prototyping phase or the agency's evaluations of the participants' performance" [1082](#cite:1082). The decisions are trial-level and not uniform, and this sweep found no Federal Circuit ruling on OT protest jurisdiction [1082](#cite:1082) [1080](#cite:1080).
applies_when: A firm challenges an OT solicitation, an OT award or a follow-on production award in a forum other than GAO [1083](#cite:1083) [1082](#cite:1082).
steps: A [SAM registration](#term:sam-gov) that lapsed between proposal submission and award ended one protest (Independent Rough Terrain Center) [1083](#cite:1083)
Objections known during the process and not raised then were held waived (Telesto) [1082](#cite:1082)
how_it_works: Space Exploration Technologies Corp. v. United States, 144 Fed. Cl. 433 (2019): no jurisdiction [1080](#cite:1080). The case went on in district court: SpaceX, No. 2:19-cv-07927-ODW (C.D. Cal. Sept. 24, 2020), protest denied on APA review [1080](#cite:1080)
Kinemetrics, Inc. v. United States, 155 Fed. Cl. 777 (2021): jurisdiction over a [CSO](#term:cso) that awarded an [IDIQ](#term:idiq) contract [1080](#cite:1080)
Hydraulics International, Inc. v. United States, 161 Fed. Cl. 167 (2022): jurisdiction over an OT contemplating [follow-on production](#term:follow-on-production) [1080](#cite:1080)

Independent Rough Terrain Center, LLC v. United States, No. 24-160 (Fed. Cl. July 1, 2024; reissued July 16, 2024): jurisdiction over a protest of a follow-on production award made under OT authority, since "nothing in the OT statutes expressly removes OT follow-on contracts from the purview of this Court's jurisdiction"; then dismissed because the protester's SAM registration lapsed between May 26 and August 9, 2023, after proposal submission and before award [1083](#cite:1083)

Raytheon Company v. United States, No. 24-1824C (Fed. Cl. Feb. 24, 2025): jurisdiction found under 28 U.S.C. 1491(b)(1); the Government's motion to dismiss a protest of a Missile Defense Agency OT award was denied [1081](#cite:1081) [1069](#cite:1069)

Telesto Group, LLC v. United States, No. 24-1784 (Fed. Cl. June 2, 2025): reviewable are compliance with [10 U.S.C. 4022](#term:prototype-ot)(d)(1)(A) (nontraditional participation), 32 [CFR](#term:cfr) Part 3, the Procurement Integrity Act, and the solicitation's terms; not reviewable are the agency's conduct of the prototyping phase and its evaluations of participants, until prototyping ends and the agency decides to proceed with a procurement; result dismissed in part, denied in part [1082](#cite:1082)

Waiver: in Telesto, objections known during the process but not raised then were waived: "it must also accept the pitfalls that accompany the exercise of that jurisdiction; the waiver rule is one of those pitfalls" [1082](#cite:1082)
On the merits in Telesto the nontraditional-participation claim failed: the Army properly relied on certifications and its own evaluation findings [1082](#cite:1082)
District courts: MD Helicopters Inc. v. United States, 435 F. Supp. 3d 1003 (D. Ariz. 2020), no district court jurisdiction [1080](#cite:1080)
An [ARPA-H](#term:arpa-h) page indexes six Court of Federal Claims decisions and one district court decision on OTs, with copies [1069](#cite:1069)

conflicts: Secondary only: CRS lists the Tucker Act (28 U.S.C. 1491) among laws that still apply to OTs [1079](#cite:1079). No primary source read in this sweep states where a performance dispute under an OT is heard.
name: Disputes during an other transaction (no Contract Disputes Act)
what: [OTs](#term:other-transaction) are not subject to the [Contract Disputes Act](#term:contract-disputes-act): "there is no statutory process for resolving disagreements about the terms or performance of the OT" [1049](#cite:1049). DoD's guide says the agreement should set its own dispute process and that counsel should advise on alternative dispute resolution [1049](#cite:1049).
applies_when: A performer and the Government disagree about the terms or performance of an OT after award [1049](#cite:1049).
steps: The dispute process is whatever the agreement states; DoD's guide says the agreement should set one [1049](#cite:1049)
how_it_works: [Research OTs](#term:research-ot): agreements should set out how either party raises a dispute and favor alternative dispute resolution [1052](#cite:1052)

DARPA's training lists the Contract Disputes Act, termination for convenience or default and the changes [clause](#term:clause-numbering) among the things that do not apply to an OT [1063](#cite:1063); [ARPA-H](#term:arpa-h)'s training lists the Contract Disputes Act [1066](#cite:1066); [NIH](#term:agency-abbreviations)'s policy guide lists it among laws that may not apply [1099](#cite:1099)

In a [consortium](#term:consortium) the member's [project agreement](#term:base-agreement) comes from the manager: under the 2017 C5 base agreement CMG issues a Project Agreement to the selected member [1224](#cite:1224). DOE's guide makes the general point: "Consortium arrangements are commercial agreements and DOE is not party to the consortium" [1093](#cite:1093)
Fiscal law still binds the Government's side of an OT: [GAO](#term:gao) applied the recording statute and the bona fide needs statute to NIH other transactions [1077](#cite:1077)
governing_text: The agreement's own disputes clause; the Contract Disputes Act does not apply

conflicts: (Synthesis flagged by the sweep) That "government purpose rights" has no meaning in an OT unless the agreement defines or imports it is the sweep's own inference from the guidebook and the clause; the definition is the clause's [1064](#cite:1064) [968](#cite:968).

Secondary only: a law-firm alert says sections 805 and 843–850 of the FY2026 NDAA address technical data for covered systems (tracking, verification, escrow); not read in primary text [1110](#cite:1110).
official_url is the ARPA-H-hosted copy of the DoD IP Guidebook (April 2025), the address swept [1064](#cite:1064).
name: Intellectual property and data rights in an other transaction (negotiated, not default)
what: [OTs](#term:other-transaction) sit outside the default IP rules: "OTs are not subject to the statutory regimes of the Bayh-Dole Act (35 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 201-212) for patentable inventions or 10 U.S.C. 3771 for technical data", and IP rights are fully negotiable [1052](#cite:1052). Nothing attaches automatically either way: "Non-FAR agreements do not automatically [grant](#term:grant) [data rights](#term:sbir-data-rights) under the funding rule. Rights need to be specifically stated in the agreement." [1064](#cite:1064). DoD's guide says "the Government has greater flexibility to negotiate IP terms for OTs than in traditional Government contracts" [1049](#cite:1049).
applies_when: Before signing any OT or consortium project agreement: the rights each side holds are those stated in the agreement [1064](#cite:1064).
steps: No official step-by-step account of how a small firm should list and mark background IP in an OT was read: Table 9 of the IP Guidebook ("Other Transactions Issue Topics and Considerations for IP", p. 54) was cut off by the fetch tool [1064](#cite:1064), as were the OT Guide's appendices [1049](#cite:1049)
how_it_works: Standard [DFARS](#term:dfars) license terms are not applicable in non-FAR agreements such as OTAs [1064](#cite:1064)

"The Bayh-Dole Act (patents) and 10 U.S.C. 3771-3775 (Rights in technical data) does not apply" [1063](#cite:1063); "IP rights are fully negotiable under all types of OTs." [1050](#cite:1050); "OTs allow for complete flexibility and freedom in negotiating rights" [1066](#cite:1066)

"Government purpose rights" is defined in the FAR-world [clause](#term:clause-numbering) DFARS 252.227-7013 (AUG 2025), which does not apply to OTs of its own force: rights to use, modify, reproduce, release, perform, display, or disclose technical data within the Government without restriction, and to release or disclose outside the Government for United States Government purposes [968](#cite:968)

In that clause government purpose rights apply to data for items developed with mixed funding, for "a 5-year period, or such other period as may be negotiated"; after that the Government has unlimited rights [968](#cite:968)

"Government purpose" in that clause means any activity in which the United States Government is a party, including cooperative agreements with international or multi-national defense organizations, or sales or transfers to foreign governments or international organizations [968](#cite:968)
An agreement can import the term: a TReX II statement of need posted in July 2024 specifies Government Purpose Rights [1163](#cite:1163)

DoD's stated principles: "Respect and protect IP resulting from technology development investments by both the private sector and the U.S. Government"; specially negotiated licenses are described as statutorily preferred where they better balance DoD and industry interests [1064](#cite:1064)
DoD may not normally share with third parties technical data in which it holds limited rights or SBIR/STTR data rights [1064](#cite:1064)
[Agreements Officers](#term:contracting-officer) are told to consult counsel and the DoD IP Cadre guidance [1049](#cite:1049)
[DIU](#term:diu) states that companies retain ownership of IP assets created during the effort [97](#cite:97), and lists data rights implications among its Phase 2 pitch factors [1065](#cite:1065)

Submitted proposals, business plans and technical information are protected from disclosure for five years after receipt ([10 U.S.C. 4021](#term:research-ot)(i)) [1030](#cite:1030); DoD's guide lists FOIA as still applicable with that five-year protection [1049](#cite:1049)
[DOE](#term:agency-abbreviations) differs: without Bayh-Dole, title to inventions would vest in DOE under its title-vesting statutes unless the agreement provides otherwise [1093](#cite:1093)
NIH: "Flexibility in the negotiation of IP rights is one of the rationales for using an OT." [1099](#cite:1099)
NSWC Crane gives flexibility on IP as one of its reasons for using the S²MARTS OTA [1153](#cite:1153)
governing_text: The agreement's own IP terms. Not applicable of their own force: Bayh-Dole Act (35 U.S.C. 201–212); 10 U.S.C. 3771–3775; DFARS 252.227-7013. 10 U.S.C. 4021(i) (five-year protection of submitted information)

name: Other transaction approval, notice and audit thresholds
what: The statute sets dollar tiers at which a [prototype OT](#term:prototype-ot) or a [follow-on production award](#term:follow-on-production) needs a written determination by a named official and notice to Congress, and a tier at which the [Comptroller General](#term:gao) gets access to records [1028](#cite:1028). The values include all options: "As indicated in section 4022 for all threshold levels, the value shall include all options." [1060](#cite:1060). The determination authority may not be delegated [1028](#cite:1028) [1060](#cite:1060).
applies_when: A prototype OT over $100,000,000; a follow-on production contract or transaction over $100,000,000; an agreement providing payments over $5,000,000 [1028](#cite:1028).
how_it_works: Over $100,000,000 but not over $500,000,000 (including all options): written determination by the head of the contracting activity (or the director, for DARPA, [DIU](#term:diu), MDA) that subsection (d) will be met and use of the authority is essential to promoting the success of the prototype project [1028](#cite:1028)

Over $500,000,000 (including all options): the senior procurement executive (or DARPA/DIU/MDA director) determines in writing that (d) will be met and use is essential to meet critical national security objectives; congressional defense committees notified in writing at least 30 days before the authority is exercised [1028](#cite:1028)

Follow-on production contract or transaction over $100,000,000 (including all options): a covered official determines in writing that (d) was met for the prior prototype transaction, (f) will be met, and use is essential to meet critical national security objectives; congressional defense committees notified at the time the authority is exercised [1028](#cite:1028)

How the tiers came about: [Pub. L.](#term:public-law) 118-159 section 816 (December 2024) moved the $100M–$500M determination to the head of the contracting activity and the over-$500M determination to the senior procurement executive [1029](#cite:1029) [1028](#cite:1028)

DoD's allocation for prototype OTs (memo of August 27, 2025, which rescinds and replaces the November 20, 2018 approval memo). Military departments: head of the contracting activity up to $100M and $100M–$500M; senior procurement executive over $500M. DARPA/DIU/MDA: head of the contracting activity up to $100M; Director above. Defense agencies, field activities and combatant commands: head of the contracting activity up to $100M; senior procurement executive $100M–$500M; USD(R&E) or USD(A&S) over $500M [1060](#cite:1060)

DoD's allocation for follow-on production: service acquisition executive (military departments); Director (DARPA/DIU/MDA); for defense agencies and combatant commands, Director or commanding officer up to $100M and USD(R&E) or USD(A&S) above [1060](#cite:1060)

Comptroller General access: a [clause](#term:clause-numbering) for agreements providing payments over $5,000,000; limits for parties with no prior audit-access agreements; three-year limit on record examination [1028]. 32 CFR 3.7 states it as total Government payments over $5,000,000, with access ending three years after final payment [1037](#cite:1037)

DoD audit access (32 [CFR](#term:cfr) 3.8): [fixed-price](#term:firm-fixed-price) OTs generally need no DoD audit access; for [cost-type](#term:cost-reimbursement-contract) OTs over $5,000,000 DoD "shall" have access for traditional contractors and "should" for nontraditional ones [1037](#cite:1037)
The Comptroller General access clause is required for Prototype or follow-on production OTs with payments over $5 million and not for [Research OTs](#term:research-ot) [1049](#cite:1049)

What oversight found: two of eleven transactions GAO reviewed lacked required higher-level review, a $7.8 million DARPA transaction and a $10 million Army Contracting Command–New Jersey transaction [1072](#cite:1072); the [Inspector General](#term:dod-ig) found contracting offices sought approval four different ways (per base ceiling, per project, per phase, per performer) [1124](#cite:1124), and its recommendation 1.e on approval levels is shown open [1125](#cite:1125)
[Consortium](#term:consortium) ceilings and projects are different numbers: 13 base OTs shown as $24.6 billion in FPDS-NG were actually 718 projects worth $8.7 billion [1124](#cite:1124)

[CSO](#term:cso) contracts under 10 [U.S.C.](#term:usc) 3458: congressional notification within 45 days of award for contracts exceeding $100,000,000 [1033] [1040]; codified DFARS 212.7003 still requires senior procurement executive approval to award a contract in excess of $100 million [1040](#cite:1040)

Civilian parallels: [BARDA](#term:barda) needs a written determination by the Assistant Secretary for Financial Resources for projects expected to cost [HHS](#term:agency-abbreviations) more than $100,000,000 [1095]; ARPA-H's cross-government table notes a CDC written determination over $40M and an IARPA cap of $75M [1066](#cite:1066)

Other reporting to Congress: annual reports on prototype OTAs since 2019 under section 873 of the FY2019 NDAA [1070](#cite:1070); "Not later than 60 days after the date on which a waiver is issued under this section, the Secretary of Defense shall provide" notice of a section 1826 waiver [1032](#cite:1032)
governing_text: 10 U.S.C. 4022(a)(2), (a)(3) and (c); USD(A&S) memorandum of August 27, 2025; 32 CFR 3.7 and 3.8; 10 U.S.C. 3458(e); DFARS 212.7003 and 212.7005
